# Japan Trip Planning

## Overview

I have now shaped a two-week Japan trip three times, once in spring and twice in autumn, and the same skeleton keeps working. Fly into Tokyo, work west by rail, finish in Osaka or Kyoto and leave from Kansai. Keep the first city loose, the middle tight and the last day empty. This note is the version I would hand to someone doing it for the first time.

## Two-Week Itinerary

Day one is arrival. Land at Haneda in the afternoon, clear immigration, pick up a pocket wifi and load a Suica card at the airport, then take the train to Shinjuku. Check into a business hotel near the station, walk a few blocks to Omoide Yokocho for grilled skewers and sleep early. The first day is always a write-off after a long flight, so plan nothing that needs a clear head.

Day two covers west Tokyo. Morning at Meiji Jingu, then the walk down Takeshita Street in Harajuku, lunch at a standing sushi bar in Shibuya, an afternoon in the record shops, and the crossing at dusk. The shrine forest is a shock of quiet after the station, and I try to reach it before eight. Day three is east Tokyo: the Tsukiji outer market for breakfast, Asakusa and Senso-ji, a museum in Ueno, and Akihabara in the evening. Buy the grilled scallops at the market and eat them standing. Day four is a day trip, either Nikko for the shrine complex or Kamakura for the coast and the big Buddha, back by dinner.

Day five is the first long rail leg. Take the Shinkansen west to Kanazawa, about two and a half hours, and spend the afternoon in the Kenrokuen garden and the old samurai district. Stay two nights, because one is not enough and the seafood market deserves a full morning. Day six continues to Kyoto, an hour or so by train, with the evening in the Gion lanes. Drop the bags first and walk, since the lanes are narrow and taxis cannot reach most doorways. Day seven is east Kyoto: temples in the Higashiyama hills, a walk up to Kiyomizu-dera at opening, and a slow lunch near the canal. Day eight is west Kyoto, Arashiyama in the early morning and the bamboo grove before the crowds, then the monkey park if the legs still work. Back in town, the food hall under Kyoto station solves a tired dinner in one stop.

Day nine is a day trip to Nara, forty-five minutes each way, for the deer park and the big temple hall. Go early, because the deer are pushy once the bus tours land and the great hall is best before the light flattens. Day ten is a long hop to Hiroshima with a ferry to Miyajima, the torii in the water and the ropeway up the mountain. Leave the suitcase in a station locker and carry one small bag for the night. Day eleven returns toward Osaka, checking into a hotel in Namba by mid-afternoon, with the evening on the Dotonbori canal. Day twelve is a full Osaka day: the Kuromon market in the morning, the castle park after lunch, and takoyaki wherever the queue looks local.

Day thirteen is the buffer. Use it for whatever got rained out, or for a slow last day of shopping and food. This is also the day to sort the final logistics, pack, and repack once so nothing fragile rides in the checked bag. As for the seats themselves, I always book Shinkansen seats the day before departure for any leg longer than two hours, because the reserved cars fill on popular routes and standing for three hours with a suitcase is a poor trade for the few minutes it takes at a ticket machine.

Day fourteen is departure from Kansai. The airport train from Namba runs often enough that I leave three hours before the flight and still arrive early. I keep the morning free for a last coffee and a supermarket run for snacks, then check in and fly home.

## Budget

Rail is the biggest line. A fourteen-day Japan Rail Pass runs about 50,000 yen and pays for itself if you make three or more long legs, which this route does. Hotels land between 9,000 and 15,000 yen a night for a business room, cheaper outside Tokyo. Food is easy to control: 1,000 yen for a good breakfast, 1,200 for lunch, and 3,000 to 5,000 for dinner with a drink. Budget 250,000 to 350,000 yen per person for two weeks on the ground, flights aside. Carry some cash; the smaller stalls and shrines still do not take cards.
